title: Stationarity as a One-Mode Constraint on Quantum Correlation
abstract: A stationary quantum state has one dynamical phase factor and one scalar energy even when its internal response spans a large Hilbert space. Our argument concerns not the value or observability of an absolute phase, but the one-ness of stationary time evolution. In regularized Hartree--Fock (reg-HF), the connection to the stationary mean field is established before any one-mode reduction: the primitive-product relative-coordinate Gaussian measure induced by the Gaussian HF representation fixes a covariance and, at that covariance, is simultaneously the minimum-Fisher-information and maximum-Shannon-differential-entropy distribution and the equality case of the Stam bound. The Coulomb operator admits a compatible Gaussian scale resolution, and virial completion converts the resulting regularized pair displacement into a stationary-compatible response. Stationarity motivates a one-mode constraint on the terminal scalar correlation response. The decisive reg-HF hypothesis is a one-mode exclusion axiom: covariance carried by response components orthogonal to the retained pair mode is excluded from the terminal scalar energy property, without asserting that the unrestricted response is one dimensional. Helium provides the minimal nontrivial test. The parameter-free retained Coulomb carrier $-δ/e$ and finite-$Z$ insertion $8δ/9$ closely reproduce independent He-like coefficients and energies, while an explicit Bethe--Goldstone calculation displays a broad non-single-denominator return spectrum even though its scalar energy is exactly moment-compressible. The result separates microscopic spectral complexity from one-mode energetic sufficiency.
summary: This theoretical work argues that for quantum systems in stationary states, the terminal scalar correlation energy can be accurately described by a single, 'one-mode' constraint, even if the full microscopic excitation spectrum is complex. By testing this hypothesis on Helium using reg-HF methods against Bethe-Goldstone theory, the authors show that energetic sufficiency does not require spectral simplicity.
main_problem: The paper investigates whether the terminal scalar correlation-energy response of a quantum system, particularly in stationary states, must retain the full dimensionality of its microscopic response.
main_result: Stationarity imposes a 'one-mode constraint' on the terminal scalar correlation response, which is shown to be highly accurate even when the full microscopic excitation spectrum (as seen in Bethe-Goldstone calculations) is complex and multi-dimensional.
method: The authors use a regularized Hartree-Fock (reg-HF) construction, employing Gaussian measures and virial completion, and contrast these results against exact calculations like Bethe-Goldstone (BG) theory.
model_or_system: The primary test case is the Helium atom/ion system. The theoretical framework involves analyzing the correlation energy derived from the Hamiltonian under the constraint of a stationary state.
key_observables: Terminal scalar correlation response ($\Delta^{(1)}_0$), Bethe-Goldstone pair correlation energy ($E_{	ext{BG}}^c$), and the diagnostic quantity $W_{BG}$ which measures spectral complexity.
important_parameters: The residual dimensionless parameter $\delta$, the retained Coulomb carrier $\delta/e$, and the finite-$Z$ insertion ratio $8\delta/9$.
main_assumptions: The core hypothesis is the 'one-mode exclusion axiom,' which assumes that covariance components orthogonal to the retained pair mode are excluded from the terminal energy property.
figures_summary: Figure 2 compares the absolute error of the one-mode He-like correlation energies against the BG spectral-width diagnostic $W_{BG}$, demonstrating a clear separation between energetic sufficiency and spectral simplicity.
paper_structure: The paper develops the argument by first establishing the reg-HF framework and the one-mode constraint imposed by stationarity. It then tests this constraint using Helium, comparing the resulting single-mode energy calculation against the full, complex spectrum derived from Bethe-Goldstone theory.
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous theoretical tool to decouple the dimensionality required for calculating a specific, observable energy (the terminal state) from the complexity of the underlying quantum correlation structure, which is highly relevant for understanding correlation in strongly interacting systems.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Logical structure of the stationary one-mode construc- tion. The HF primitive-product Gaussian measure identifies a minimum-information relative-pair mode, the compatible Coulomb scale channel supplies the interaction response, and the virial supplies its stationary kinetic completion. Stationar- ity then motivates Eq. (11), which relinquishes response-space completeness for the terminal energy property. The dashed branch emphasizes that microscopic multimode structure is not claimed to disappear.

FIG. 2. Helium separates one-mode energetic sufficiency from microscopic spectral simplicity. Left: absolute error of the parameter-free one-mode He-like correlation energies over representative nuclear charges; the comparison uses high-accuracy numerical/Laguerre-based Hartree–Fock reference energies rather than a finite Gaussian orbital basis. Right: the BG spectral- width diagnostic WBG for an independent one-center spherical-Gaussian calculation (representative radial space 18s, 12p, 10d, 8f) remains near unity rather than zero, demonstrating a broad non-single-denominator return spectrum.
